name: incomplete_kernel_proof

input.source:
PDF page 1:
Linear maps and their kernels
Definition 1. A map T from a real vector space V to a real vector space W is linear if T(u+v)=T(u)+T(v) for
every u,v in V, and T(av)=aT(v) for every real scalar a and v in V. The kernel of T is ker(T)={v in
V:T(v)=0_W}.
Definition 2. A subset U of V is a subspace if it contains 0_V, is closed under addition, and is closed under
real scalar multiplication.
Theorem 1. The kernel of a linear map is a subspace of its domain.
Proof. Scalar preservation gives T(0_V)=T(0v)=0T(v)=0_W, so 0_V is in ker(T). If u and v are in ker(T),
then T(u+v)=T(u)+T(v)=0_W+0_W=0_W, so u+v is in ker(T). If a is any real scalar and v is in ker(T), then
T(av)=aT(v)=a0_W=0_W, so av is in ker(T). These three properties establish the subspace claim.
Example. For T(x,y)=x, the kernel is {(0,y):y is real}, a subspace of R^2. Checking finitely many vectors
cannot prove the general closure conditions.
Counterexample to removing linearity. The nonlinear map f(x)=x^2-1 has zero set {-1,1}, which does not
contain zero and is not a subspace of R.
input.question: Constructed proof-repair task: let $T:V\to W$ be linear between real vector spaces and let $K=\ker(T)$. A proposed proof says: 'Since $0_V\in K$, $T(0_V)=0_W$. Choose one $v\in K$. We have $T(v+v)=0_W$ and $T(2v)=0_W$, so $K$ is a subspace.' Explain why the opening is circular and why the remaining checks do not establish the required closure conditions. Replace the proposed proof with a complete ordered argument using Definition 2. Justify every equality and each membership conclusion.
gradingCriteria: Identifies the circular assumption of zero membership and explains why the selected addition and scalar checks do not establish universal closure.
States the real vector-space and linearity hypotheses and recognizes $K\subseteq V$.
Derives $T(0_V)=0_W$ from scalar preservation without assuming kernel membership, justifying each equality and then concluding $0_V\in K$.
Uses arbitrary $u,v\in K$, establishes $u+v\in V$, and justifies the complete additivity calculation and kernel membership conclusion.
Uses arbitrary $a\in\mathbb{R}$ and $v\in K$, establishes $av\in V$, and justifies the complete scalar-preservation calculation and kernel membership conclusion.
Concludes that Definition 2 applies because all three required conditions have been established.
input.expectedAnswer:
The opening assumes $0_V\in K$, which is exactly the first subspace condition still needing proof. Although kernel membership would imply $T(0_V)=0_W$, it cannot be used to establish that membership without an independent derivation. The remaining checks cover only adding a particular vector to itself and multiplying it by the particular scalar $2$. Addition closure requires every pair of kernel vectors, and scalar closure requires every kernel vector and every real scalar. The proposed argument also has not yet independently established that a kernel vector exists.

A valid replacement is:

1. By the kernel definition, $K\subseteq V$. Choose $z=0_V\in V$, which exists because $V$ is a vector space. Since $0z=0_V$, scalar preservation gives $T(0_V)=T(0z)=0T(z)=0_W$. The first equality uses $0z=0_V$; the second applies scalar preservation to $z\in V$ and $0\in\mathbb{R}$; the third uses $T(z)\in W$ and the vector-space rule for multiplication by zero. Consequently, $0_V\in V$ has image $0_W$, so the kernel definition gives $0_V\in K$.

2. Let $u,v\in K$ be arbitrary. The kernel definition gives $u,v\in V$ and $T(u)=T(v)=0_W$. Since $V$ is a vector space, $u+v\in V$. Now $T(u+v)=T(u)+T(v)=0_W+0_W=0_W$. The first equality applies additivity to $u,v\in V$; the second substitutes their kernel images; the third uses the additive identity in $W$. The kernel definition therefore gives $u+v\in K$. Because $u,v$ were arbitrary, $K$ is closed under addition.

3. Let $a\in\mathbb{R}$ and $v\in K$ be arbitrary. The kernel definition gives $v\in V$ and $T(v)=0_W$. Since $V$ is a real vector space, $av\in V$. Now $T(av)=aT(v)=a0_W=0_W$. The first equality applies scalar preservation to $a\in\mathbb{R}$ and $v\in V$; the second substitutes the kernel image; the third uses the rule that any scalar times the zero vector is the zero vector. The kernel definition therefore gives $av\in K$. Since both choices were arbitrary, $K$ is closed under real scalar multiplication.

Thus $K\subseteq V$ contains $0_V$ and satisfies both universal closure conditions. Definition 2 establishes that $K$ is a subspace of $V$.

Full credit requires both identifying the defects and supplying the complete replacement argument; describing the defects alone does not establish the theorem.
input.studentAnswer: The kernel contains zero, so it is a subspace.

expectedReasoning: Zero membership alone proves neither universal closure condition.

Do not assume that $U_b$ contains a vector.

Independently derives $T(0_V)=0_W$ from scalar preservation and justifies every equality without assuming $U_b$ is nonempty.
Proves the forward direction using zero membership from the subspace definition and $T(0_V)=b$ from the definition of $U_b$.
Explains why $b\ne0_W$ rules out a subspace through failure of zero membership, including the possibility that $U_b$ is empty.
Under $b=0_W$, establishes zero membership and proves addition closure for arbitrary $u,v\in U_b$, justifying domain membership and every image equality.
Under $b=0_W$, proves scalar closure for arbitrary $a\in\mathbb{R}$ and $v\in U_b$, justifying domain membership and every image equality.
Invokes all three subspace conditions to conclude the reverse direction and explicitly concludes the equivalence.

Let $V,W$ be real vector spaces, let $T:V\to W$ be linear, and fix an arbitrary $b\in W$. By definition, $U_b\subseteq V$.

First derive preservation of zero independently of $U_b$. Choose $z=0_V\in V$. Then $T(0_V)=T(0z)=0T(z)=0_W$. The first equality uses the vector-space identity $0z=0_V$; the second uses scalar preservation with $0\in\mathbb{R}$ and $z\in V$; the third uses $T(z)\in W$ and multiplication by zero in $W$.

For the forward direction, suppose $U_b$ is a subspace of $V$. Definition 2 gives $0_V\in U_b$. The definition of $U_b$ then gives $T(0_V)=b$. Combining this equation with the independently established equation $T(0_V)=0_W$ yields $b=0_W$. This argument does not assume that an arbitrary preimage of $b$ exists: zero membership follows from the subspace hypothesis itself. In particular, if $b\ne0_W$, then $T(0_V)=0_W\ne b$, so $0_V\notin U_b$ and $U_b$ cannot be a subspace, whether it is empty or nonempty.

For the reverse direction, suppose $b=0_W$. Because $0_V\in V$ and $T(0_V)=0_W=b$, the definition of $U_b$ gives $0_V\in U_b$.

Let $u,v\in U_b$ be arbitrary. Their membership gives $u,v\in V$ and $T(u)=b=0_W$, $T(v)=b=0_W$. Since $V$ is a vector space, $u+v\in V$. Additivity, substitution of these images, and the additive identity in $W$ give $T(u+v)=T(u)+T(v)=0_W+0_W=0_W=b$. Thus $u+v\in U_b$ by its definition. Because the pair was arbitrary, addition closure holds.

Let $a\in\mathbb{R}$ and $v\in U_b$ be arbitrary. Membership gives $v\in V$ and $T(v)=b=0_W$. Since $V$ is a real vector space, $av\in V$. Scalar preservation, substitution of the image, and scalar multiplication of the zero vector give $T(av)=aT(v)=a0_W=0_W=b$. Thus $av\in U_b$ by its definition. Because the scalar and vector were arbitrary, real scalar closure holds.

Therefore, when $b=0_W$, the subset $U_b$ contains zero and satisfies both closure conditions, so Definition 2 makes it a subspace of $V$. Both directions have been proved, establishing the equivalence for every $b\in W$.

Full credit requires a valid argument in both directions, including the zero derivation and the universal closure arguments. Merely recognizing $U_0$ as the kernel does not supply the requested reconstruction.

input.question: Constructed transfer task: let $T:V\to W$ be linear between real vector spaces. For a fixed but arbitrary $b\in W$, define $U_b=\{v\in V:T(v)=b\}$. Prove that $U_b$ is a subspace of $V$ if and only if $b=0_W$. Derive preservation of zero from scalar preservation, prove both directions, and justify every equality and membership conclusion. Do not assume that $U_b$ contains a vector.
gradingCriteria: States the real vector-space and linearity hypotheses, treats $b\in W$ as arbitrary, and notes $U_b\subseteq V$.
Independently derives $T(0_V)=0_W$ from scalar preservation and justifies every equality without assuming $U_b$ is nonempty.
Proves the forward direction using zero membership from the subspace definition and $T(0_V)=b$ from the definition of $U_b$.
Explains why $b\ne0_W$ rules out a subspace through failure of zero membership, including the possibility that $U_b$ is empty.
Under $b=0_W$, establishes zero membership and proves addition closure for arbitrary $u,v\in U_b$, justifying domain membership and every image equality.
Under $b=0_W$, proves scalar closure for arbitrary $a\in\mathbb{R}$ and $v\in U_b$, justifying domain membership and every image equality.
Invokes all three subspace conditions to conclude the reverse direction and explicitly concludes the equivalence.
input.expectedAnswer:
Let $V,W$ be real vector spaces, let $T:V\to W$ be linear, and fix an arbitrary $b\in W$. By definition, $U_b\subseteq V$.

First derive preservation of zero independently of $U_b$. Choose $z=0_V\in V$. Then $T(0_V)=T(0z)=0T(z)=0_W$. The first equality uses the vector-space identity $0z=0_V$; the second uses scalar preservation with $0\in\mathbb{R}$ and $z\in V$; the third uses $T(z)\in W$ and multiplication by zero in $W$.

For the forward direction, suppose $U_b$ is a subspace of $V$. Definition 2 gives $0_V\in U_b$. The definition of $U_b$ then gives $T(0_V)=b$. Combining this equation with the independently established equation $T(0_V)=0_W$ yields $b=0_W$. This argument does not assume that an arbitrary preimage of $b$ exists: zero membership follows from the subspace hypothesis itself. In particular, if $b\ne0_W$, then $T(0_V)=0_W\ne b$, so $0_V\notin U_b$ and $U_b$ cannot be a subspace, whether it is empty or nonempty.

For the reverse direction, suppose $b=0_W$. Because $0_V\in V$ and $T(0_V)=0_W=b$, the definition of $U_b$ gives $0_V\in U_b$.

Let $u,v\in U_b$ be arbitrary. Their membership gives $u,v\in V$ and $T(u)=b=0_W$, $T(v)=b=0_W$. Since $V$ is a vector space, $u+v\in V$. Additivity, substitution of these images, and the additive identity in $W$ give $T(u+v)=T(u)+T(v)=0_W+0_W=0_W=b$. Thus $u+v\in U_b$ by its definition. Because the pair was arbitrary, addition closure holds.

Let $a\in\mathbb{R}$ and $v\in U_b$ be arbitrary. Membership gives $v\in V$ and $T(v)=b=0_W$. Since $V$ is a real vector space, $av\in V$. Scalar preservation, substitution of the image, and scalar multiplication of the zero vector give $T(av)=aT(v)=a0_W=0_W=b$. Thus $av\in U_b$ by its definition. Because the scalar and vector were arbitrary, real scalar closure holds.

Therefore, when $b=0_W$, the subset $U_b$ contains zero and satisfies both closure conditions, so Definition 2 makes it a subspace of $V$. Both directions have been proved, establishing the equivalence for every $b\in W$.

Full credit requires a valid argument in both directions, including the zero derivation and the universal closure arguments. Merely recognizing $U_0$ as the kernel does not supply the requested reconstruction.
